failure_modes.description: Assumption that intersections can communicate reliably with immediate neighbors is unrealistic in current infrastructure
failure_modes.evidence: Most traffic signal infrastructure is decades old and lacks reliable communication capabilities between intersections

failure_modes.description: Distributed consensus algorithms have proven too slow for real-time traffic control
failure_modes.evidence: Existing distributed systems like blockchain consensus take seconds to minutes, while traffic signals need millisecond-level response times

failure_modes.description: The system would fail at network boundaries where intersections have different numbers of neighbors
failure_modes.evidence: Uneven network topology would create convergence issues at intersections with fewer neighbors, creating bottlenecks

failure_modes.description: Similar approaches have been attempted and failed in the past
failure_modes.evidence: Previous distributed traffic signal systems like SCATS and SCOOT have shown limited success and mostly rely on centralized coordination

failure_modes.description: The proposed system would be overwhelmed by communication overhead
failure_modes.evidence: Each intersection would need to communicate with all neighbors, creating O(n^2) communication complexity that scales poorly with network size

failure_modes.description: Traffic signals require deterministic timing for safety, while consensus algorithms are probabilistic
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic signals must guarantee minimum green times for pedestrian safety, which probabilistic consensus cannot guarantee
